title: Adaptive throttles, KV prefetch, and max_seq capacity planning
meeting_header:
Date: 2026-08-04T14:00:00Z
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Sofia Martinez (Redwood SE), Arjun Patel (Redwood Eng); Claire Huang (NimbusPay - Platform Eng), Roberto Silva (NimbusPay - CTO), Maya Khan (NimbusPay - SRE)
Location: Zoom call
Notes: SE-led throughput scoping for on-prem/VPC deployment; focus on continuous batching and max_num_seqs sizing.
summary: Deep technical scoping with NimbusPay on throughput knobs: continuous batching behavior, max_num_seqs sizing for their mixed token distribution, KV cache prefetch strategy for bursty user queries, token caps to protect tail latency, and VPC constraints for on-prem validation. Agreed next steps to run mixed workload benchmarks and share knob matrix.
topics: KV cache prefetch vs lazy load
action_items: Sofia Martinez|Run mixed workload benchmark (64/512/4k token mix) on dev cluster and collect p50/p95/p99|2026-08-11
Arjun Patel|Create knob matrix with recommended defaults and safe ranges for max_num_seqs, max_tokens_in_flight, token_ceiling|2026-08-09
Claire Huang|Provision VPC test cluster and share access details + sample traffic profile|2026-08-07
next_steps: Redwood to deliver scheduler knob spreadsheet and short runbook (link to doc)
Customer to provision VPC test cluster and upload traces
Run 48-hour soak test with kv-prefetch enabled and report regression metrics
questions: What should we set for max_num_seqs given our 1% 4k token tail?
How aggressive is prefetch eviction during bursts?
How does quantization affect kernel selection for long sequences?
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): ok everyone thanks for joining, quick agenda — we'll go through scheduler knobs, continuous batching behavior, kv prefetch patterns, and then plan the benchmark. hi NimbusPay folks, can you confirm the traffic profile?
[00:18] Claire (NimbusPay): yeah, hi, thanks. so prime traffic is web checkout flows ~60 tokens per request mostly but we do have very rare long sessions, maybe 0.8-1% that run 2k-4k tokens for dispute resolution chat.
[00:35] Sofia (Redwood SE): got it. that's the important part, those tails drive resource pressure. we'll talk about max_num_seqs and token ceilings to bound that.
[00:47] Roberto (NimbusPay): to be clear we want low p99 latency for checkout paths (<=300ms) but can tolerate higher for long sessions, but cost is also a factor so dedicated vs hosted trade off.
[01:03] Jordan (Redwood): yep tradeoffs noted. quick note: our continuous batching will merge short with long to a degree unless you set max_num_seqs and token caps; otherwise long seqs can prevent slot turnover and increase tail.
[01:20] Maya (NimbusPay): does kv prefetch help there, i mean pre-warming the key value cache for likely next tokens?
[01:28] Sofia (Redwood SE): in practice prefetch helps when you have repeated prefixes or conversational context reuse. for random long sessions it's hit-or-miss. we also have a prefetch policy: windowed prefetch up to N tokens ahead and an eviction priority favoring short-lived prefixes.
[01:45] Claire (NimbusPay): is that configurable? we have compliance constraints so we'd prefer to keep everything in VPC.
[01:51] Arjun (Redwood Eng): yes configurable — prefetch window, max_prefetch_per_request, and kv_hitrate_target. on VPC you'll get same knobs; network MTU and latency to cold storage can affect prefetch efficacy though.
[02:09] Jordan (Redwood): quick sketch: recommended defaults for your mix: max_num_seqs = 64 per slot, token_ceiling=1024 for checkout route, and a separate route for long sessions with max_num_seqs=8 and token_ceiling=8192. this isolates long tails.
[02:31] Roberto (NimbusPay): 64 seems high for checkout, will that starve other requests?
[02:36] Sofia (Redwood SE): it's about throughput. continuous batcher collects up to max_num_seqs then packs by seq lengths; with 60-token requests a 64-slot packing keeps GPU util high and avg latency low. but if you want lower p99, reduce to 32 and enable aggressive token_ceiling. there's a cost-latency sweetspot table we'll share.
[02:58] Claire (NimbusPay): can you explain token_ceiling again?
[03:02] Sofia (Redwood SE): token_ceiling prevents a single request from occupying a slot beyond X tokens. once a request hits the token_ceiling we either evict it to a lower priority pool or fallback to a single-request path — this avoids head-of-line blocking. it's not perfect transcription sorry, token ceiling sometimes reported as token cap in some older docs.
[03:24] Maya (NimbusPay): and quantization — does int8 make long seqs faster? we saw mixed results on our benchmarking.
[03:31] Arjun (Redwood Eng): quantization reduces memory bandwidth for attention kernels but kernel selection can change behavior. int8 gives throughput wins for shorter sequences; for very long sequences you may be memory-bound on KV cache operations where float16 with fused kernels could be better. basically test.
[03:52] Jordan (Redwood): note: for on-prem we also consider NICs and RoCE settings. large tensors cause packetization overhead; check MTU and batch serialization. perfect example — one customer had 30ms tail spikes until they bumped MTU and tuned RoCE retries.
[04:12] Roberto (NimbusPay): our infra team is worried about eviction storms when prefetch is aggressive. any guardrails?
[04:20] Sofia (Redwood SE): yes, we have prefetch rate-limiters and an eviction hysteresis window. knobs: max_prefetch_per_slot, prefetch_backoff_ms, kv_eviction_hysteresis. set conservative values for initial run: max_prefetch_per_slot=8, prefetch_backoff_ms=200, hysteresis=1s. we'll include these in the spreadsheet.
[04:45] Claire (NimbusPay): can you walk through a sample flow for a burst?
[04:49] Sofia (Redwood SE): sure. imagine 200 concurrent short checkouts and 2 long sessions. continuous batcher groups shorts into multiple slots; if a long session arrives it will be admitted only if free slots exist or it will be routed to a lower-priority lane. the scheduler governor enforces percent slots reserved for low-latency routes. there's also adaptive throttling: when avg seq length per slot increases above threshold, we reduce admission for long route.
[05:25] Jordan (Redwood): interjection: sometimes the transcription says governor but some docs call it 'seq-governor' or 'priority governor' — same thing.
[05:35] Maya (NimbusPay): how do we pick max_num_seqs for the long-session route?
[05:40] Arjun (Redwood Eng): small number, like 4-8, to keep memory and kernel efficiency manageable. we use fewer seqs so the kernel path for long sequences is optimized for long-run attention and kv streaming. too many and you lose per-seq throughput.
[05:56] Claire (NimbusPay): i want to see results for mixed mixes — can you simulate our distribution?
[06:00] Sofia (Redwood SE): yes we'll run a mixed workload: 90% 60-token, 9% 512-token, 1% 4k-token. we'll instrument p50/p95/p99 and token-cost per request.
[06:14] Jordan (Redwood): note on slot packing heuristics — we have hybrid packing: if sequences are similar length they get packed tighter; otherwise we use sequence padding heuristics. the scheduler also uses lookahead to avoid packing very long with very short where it would increase wasted compute.
[06:35] Customer (Roberto): any notes about warm vs cold kv cache? we see cold misses impact p99 badly.
[06:42] Sofia (Redwood SE): yes, cold misses are expensive. two mitigations: prefix-based prefetch and sticky KV lanes for conversational sessions. sticky lane pins a session's KV shard to same GPU to improve hit rate; requires affinity but reduces cold fetches. downside: less flexible scheduling.
[06:59] Claire (NimbusPay): affinity sounds risky for multi-tenant. we run many tenants per cluster.
[07:03] Arjun (Redwood Eng): you can use per-customer affinity only on Dedicated or Private clusters; in hosted we avoid strong affinity because of multi-tenancy. for your VPC test we'll show the trade-offs.
[07:18] Jordan (Redwood): quick break — any blockers for us to run initial benchmarks?
[07:21] Claire (NimbusPay): we need the spreadsheet and an instruction set for generating the traffic. also we need an estimate of cost for the soak.
[07:28] Jordan (Redwood): will provide knob sheet and a rough cost estimate. link to runbook: [redwood internal runbook link placeholder].
[07:36] Sofia (Redwood SE): diving deeper: scheduler knobs you should care about — max_num_seqs, max_tokens_in_flight, token_ceiling, priority_window_ms, prefetch_backoff_ms. recommended safe starting values attached in action items.
[07:54] Maya (NimbusPay): max_tokens_in_flight? I haven't seen that before.
[07:57] Arjun (Redwood Eng): it's a global cap on total tokens being processed concurrently on a worker. prevents memory blowouts when many medium sequences line up. if you set it too low you throttle overall throughput; too high and you risk OOM. set based on GPU memory and expected max_seq lengths.
[08:16] Claire (NimbusPay): ok good. on quantization again, our concerns on hallucinations — does quant change output determinism?
[08:21] Sofia (Redwood SE): minor differences can appear with aggressive quant; we usually recommend eval on a held-out prompt set. Redwood Optimize has a module to compare quality regression vs token-cost delta. we'll run that on your prompts.
[08:36] Jordan (Redwood): crosstalk moment — sorry, I saw a question in chat: "what about bursting to a cheaper model?"
[08:41] Arjun (Redwood Eng): model fallback is supported — route long non-critical sessions to a cheaper quantized variant. you can also define cost-based policy to automated fallback during high utilisation. caveat: model outputs may differ and you need evals for acceptance.
[09:00] Claire (NimbusPay): security: we need SOC2 audit logs and KMS integration for Private. are there any perf implications?
[09:07] Jordan (Redwood): KMS adds a tiny latency on key fetch for cold starts; negligible for steady-state but show up in cold-start p99. audit logs have storage cost but no runtime impact. we'll share the security docs.
[09:21] Roberto (NimbusPay): any network tuning tips for VPC?
[09:25] Sofia (Redwood SE): yes: MTU, RoCE settings, and reducing serialization overhead by co-locating worker + KV store on same subnet. also consider local SSDs for KV shard persistence to avoid network round trips.
[09:41] Claire (NimbusPay): for the benchmark, do you recommend enabling kv-prefetch or starting disabled?
[09:46] Sofia (Redwood SE): start with prefetch off to establish baseline, then enable conservative prefetch to measure improvement. we'll run A/B. prefer to enable sticky lanes only in second phase.
[09:58] Jordan (Redwood): odd transcription note - sometimes the system writes "K V cash" — ignore that.
[10:05] Maya (NimbusPay): what about guardrails to prevent long sessions from hogging all reserved slots?
[10:10] Sofia (Redwood SE): use per-route reservations and dynamic reclaim. set reservation_fraction for checkout route to 0.6 and allow reclaimed slots after reclaim_window_ms=500. also use token_ceiling to bound per-request token consumption.
[10:30] Jordan (Redwood): Operationally we'll also suggest a circuit-breaker: when overall p99 for the checkout route hits threshold, automatically divert new long sessions to fallback model or queue them.
[10:46] Roberto (NimbusPay): do you have telemetry names we should watch?
[10:50] Arjun (Redwood Eng): yes: slot_fill_rate, avg_seq_length_per_slot, kv_hitrate, tokens_in_flight, prefetch_evictions_per_minute, p99_latency_route. we'll send a Grafana dashboard template.
[11:07] Claire (NimbusPay): sounds good. i want to record expected outcomes: reduce checkout p99 under 300ms while keeping % token-cost increase < 8%.
[11:16] Jordan (Redwood): agreed measurable SLO.
[11:20] Sofia (Redwood SE): ok next, scheduling of the run — we should do an initial 6h test with synthetic load then a 48h soak with production-like traces. Watch for eviction storms and increasing prefetch evictions.
[11:35] Maya (NimbusPay): how about metrics for KV prefetch effectiveness?
[11:38] Arjun (Redwood Eng): kv_prefetch_hitrate_by_prefix, eviction_latency, and cold_fetch_pct. those tell you if prefetch buys you p99 wins.
[11:50] Jordan (Redwood): wrap-up: we'll deliver knob sheet, run instructions, and cost estimate. customer will provision VPC cluster and share traces. action items assigned.
[12:05] Claire (NimbusPay): thanks Jordan, Sofia — we'll aim to have infra ready by next week.
[12:12] Jordan (Redwood): great, we'll follow up by email and attach the spreadsheet. end of call.
